name: QEMU
summary: A machine emulator and virtualizer that assembles configurable machine models from CPU, memory, device, storage, and networking components while selecting between software emulation and host accelerators.

features.name: Composable machine model
features.description: QEMU system emulation models a guest machine as a composition of CPU, memory, machine type, devices, backends, and interfaces; the selected machine and device configuration determines the guest-visible hardware topology.
benefits: Supports many guest architectures and machine types
Allows storage, networking, and device topologies to be assembled per workload
costs: Configuration compatibility depends on the selected architecture and machine type
A broad device model increases implementation and validation surface

features.name: Pluggable execution accelerators
features.description: QEMU can execute guest CPUs through software translation with TCG or delegate supported virtualization work to host accelerators such as KVM, while retaining the machine and device model around that execution path.
benefits: Provides portability when hardware virtualization is unavailable
Can use host virtualization support when it is available
costs: Performance and feature availability vary by accelerator, host, and guest architecture
The accelerator boundary adds host-specific behavior to the execution model

features.name: QOM-based device composition
features.description: The QEMU Object Model registers dynamically creatable types with single inheritance, stateless interfaces, properties, and device lifecycle hooks; the QOM tree represents the objects that make up a machine.
benefits: Provides reusable type and interface boundaries for machine components
Makes device creation and lifecycle behavior inspectable through a common model
costs: Inheritance and lifecycle hooks introduce ordering and ownership constraints
The object model does not remove device-specific correctness obligations

features.name: Machine management boundary
features.description: QEMU exposes monitor interfaces including the versioned, machine-usable QEMU Machine Protocol for external tools to inspect and control virtual machines.
benefits: Separates machine control from the process that runs the guest
costs: Management clients must track the protocol and machine configuration they use
Dynamic device changes can alter the guest-visible topology

mathematical_views.question: How does a configured virtual machine connect guest-visible devices to host execution and I/O backends?
assumptions: Machine, device, backend, and accelerator nodes are represented explicitly
Edges describe configuration or ownership rather than guaranteeing runtime success
The selected machine type and target architecture constrain valid configurations

mathematical_views.question: How can QEMU represent a machine as dynamically registered device types with lifecycle transitions?
assumptions: QOM inheritance and interfaces define reusable type relationships
Realize and unrealize transitions are treated as lifecycle edges
The QOM tree is a structural model and does not by itself prove device behavior

mathematical_views.question: What changes when the same machine model selects TCG, KVM, or another accelerator?
assumptions: Accelerator selection is a state component of VM startup
The host exposes the capabilities required by the selected accelerator
Performance equivalence between accelerators is not assumed

benefits: Broad hardware and guest compatibility through explicit machine composition
costs: More configuration dimensions and device interactions must be validated
Host-specific accelerator semantics and fallback differences

benefits: Reusable type boundaries and common device lifecycle conventions
costs: Lifecycle ordering and polymorphic dispatch increase reasoning overhead
Protocol and topology compatibility become part of integration work
